content.title: About
content.content: Cereal, cooked, NFS (3122) is a ready‑to‑eat product made from whole grains that have been heat‑treated to enhance flavor and digestibility. The flakes are soft, carry a light toasted grain aroma, and are suitable as a stand‑alone breakfast or as an addition to milk, yogurt, or smoothies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thermal processing retains most nutrients while making them more bioavailable.
NFS stands for “Not From Scratch,” meaning the product is ready to eat without further cooking.
Cereal flakes are popular in sports nutrition for their quick energy release.
The blend may include wheat, oats, barley, and rye, providing a broader amino‑acid profile.
When stored properly, the flakes stay crunchy for up to 12 months.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide a steady energy supply and help maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and contributes to gut health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, and B6 are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium, and zinc in the flakes support blood formation and immune function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The product fits low‑fat diets while still delivering nutrients.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may react to the product.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Large portions can cause a rapid rise in blood glucose.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some varieties contain added sugar; choose unsweetened versions if monitoring calorie intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the flakes dry, or add them to milk, kefir, yogurt, or plant‑based drinks. They can also be used in baking, as a coating, or in energy bars. For a softer texture, pour hot water or milk over the flakes and let them sit for 2–3 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For extended shelf life, store in the refrigerator to preserve crunchiness and prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: A cheeseburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a medium beef patty, melted cheese, fresh vegetables, sauce, and a bun. It is quick to prepare and popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheeseburger appeared in the United States in the 1920s.
There are more than 50 topping variations, including bacon, fried onions, and a range of sauces.
In Japan, cheeseburgers are often served with teriyaki sauce and seaweed.
The world’s largest cheeseburger weighed over 300 kg and was made in the US in 2012.
Cheeseburgers are frequently used in advertising as a symbol of quick, affordable food.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese supply B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates provides a quick energy boost.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheeseburgers are calorie‑dense due to fats and carbs, so they should be eaten in moderation, especially for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fat and sodium
items.content: High levels of saturated fat and salt can raise cholesterol and blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Undercooked or low‑quality meat can harbor bacteria; ensure the patty is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheeseburgers are typically eaten with the hands, holding the bottom bun. They are often served with fries, a dipping sauce, or a beverage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in plastic. Reheat in an oven or microwave to keep the bun from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: The Double cheeseburger from Burger King is a classic burger featuring two beef patties, two slices of cheese, pickles, onions, ketchup and mustard, all sandwiched between a soft sesame seed bun.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Double cheeseburger was introduced to the Burger King menu in the early 2000s as a response to growing demand for a more "meaty" option.
The burger contains roughly 450 kcal, making it more calorie‑dense than a standard cheeseburger.
The core ingredients stay the same worldwide, though minor regional variations exist.
In some markets Burger King offers a version with extra BBQ sauce or bacon.
The sesame bun is lightly toasted to give it a subtle nutty aroma.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Two beef patties provide about 30 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: The cheese adds calcium, which supports bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef supplies vitamin B12 and B6, important for nervous system function.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of readily absorbable iron, needed for blood formation.

items.title: Energy
items.content: The combination of calories, protein, and fat makes the burger a quick source of energy.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: The large amount of calories and saturated fat can contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Ketchup, mustard and processed ingredients raise the sodium content, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The burger contains dairy (cheese), gluten (bun) and may have soy traces in sauces.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked beef poses a risk of salmonella or other bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The Double cheeseburger is typically served in its branded wrapper. Eat it by hand, often accompanied by fries and a drink. You can customize with extra sauce, vegetables, or request a gluten‑free bun.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If not consumed immediately, store the burger in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat using an oven or grill to keep the bun from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg omelets and scrambled eggs are made from chicken eggs, which provide high‑quality protein, B‑group vitamins, vitamin D, and minerals such as iron, zinc, and selenium. Eggs can be prepared in many ways: beaten and cooked as an omelet, stirred and fried as scrambled eggs, or simply boiled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable and nutrient‑dense foods worldwide.
Domestication of chickens for egg production dates back over 7,000 years in Southeast Asia.
The yolk contains almost all the vitamins of the B‑group, as well as vitamins A and D.
A typical large chicken egg weighs about 50 g, with roughly 30 % white and 70 % yolk.
Eggs serve as a binding, emulsifying, and leavening agent in many culinary applications.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs provide all essential amino acids, making them a complete protein for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both yolk and white contain B2, B5, B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Choline
items.content: Eggs are one of the best dietary sources of choline, important for brain function and liver health.

items.title: Lutein and zeaxanthin
items.content: These carotenoids in the yolk help maintain eye health and reduce the risk of age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Eggs contain virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg allergy is common in children and can range from skin reactions to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: A single yolk contains about 186 mg of cholesterol; individuals with high cholesterol may limit yolk intake.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella; use pasteurized eggs or cook thoroughly.

items.title: Biotin interference
items.content: Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin and can cause deficiency if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prepare omelets or scrambled eggs in a lightly oiled pan, adding vegetables, cheese, ham, or herbs. They are suitable for breakfast, lunch, or dinner and can be incorporated into salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggs in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in their original carton. Fresh eggs keep for 3‑4 weeks. Cooked omelets should be consumed within 2‑3 days when kept in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Gravy made with soy sauce is a thick, aromatic sauce created by reducing broth, soy sauce, sugar, and spices. The recipe was first recorded in 1921 and has since become a versatile condiment for meats, potatoes, and rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial soy‑sauce gravy recipe appeared in the United States in 1921.
Soy sauce gives the gravy a distinctive umami flavor and dark color.
Gravy is often used in fusion cuisine, blending Eastern and Western traditions.
To achieve a thicker consistency, starch or flour is sometimes added.
Vegetarian versions replace meat broth with mushroom or vegetable stock.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy sauce provides plant‑based protein that can boost the nutritional profile of the dish.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Fermented products like soy sauce contain antioxidants that help protect cells.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fermentation improves the bioavailability of certain nutrients.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: When sugar is used sparingly, the gravy remains relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Soy sauce is a good source of iron, magnesium, and potassium, important for metabolism.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Soy sauce is salty, so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: Glutamate content
items.content: The gravy may contain added monosodium glutamate, which can cause headaches in sensitive people.

items.title: Calorie increase with sugar
items.content: Excessive sugar raises the calorie count of the sauce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot soy‑sauce gravy over roasted meat, chicken, fish, mashed potatoes, rice, or vegetables. It can also be used as a base for braising or as a dipping sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared gravy in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions; bring to a boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni in creamy cheese sauce is a ready‑to‑eat dish made of boiled macaroni coated with a rich, smooth cheese sauce. It is popular as a quick lunch or dinner and can be reheated in the microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became a comfort‑food icon.
Short pasta shapes such as elbows or shells are traditionally used because they hold the sauce well.
The creamy sauce is usually made from butter, milk and flour (roux) to achieve a velvety texture.
Cheddar, mozzarella or a blend of cheeses are commonly used, giving the dish its characteristic flavor.
Some regional versions add mustard or paprika for a subtle kick.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Macaroni provides complex carbohydrates that release glucose slowly, supplying sustained energy.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Hard cheeses are rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Cheese and optional meat or chicken additions increase the dish’s protein, supporting tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain macaroni, when used, contains B1, B2 and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Fatty acids
items.content: Butter in the sauce supplies saturated fats that can serve as an energy source when consumed in moderation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The combination of butter, cream and cheese makes the dish calorie‑dense, so portion control is important.

items.title: Saturated fat and cholesterol
items.content: Butter and cheese contain saturated fats that may raise cholesterol levels if eaten excessively.

items.title: Lactose and dairy protein
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or dairy allergies should choose lactose‑free or dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese can be high in salt; those with hypertension should opt for low‑sodium varieties.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional macaroni contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Cook the macaroni until al dente, drain, and set aside. Make the cheese sauce by melting butter, whisking in flour, then gradually adding milk and shredded cheese, stirring until thickened. Toss the pasta with the sauce and heat for 2‑3 minutes. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs or extra cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or cream to restore sauce consistency. Freezing is not recommended, as the sauce may separate.

macaroni-with-tuna-puerto-rican-style.title: Macaroni with Tuna, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: A classic Puerto Rican comfort food, macaroni with tuna combines cooked pasta with canned tuna, tomato sauce, olive oil, garlic, onion, sweet pepper, and spices such as oregano and cumin. The dish is quick to prepare, hearty, and carries a bright, slightly spicy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish emerged in the mid‑20th century when canned tuna became widely available in Puerto Rico.
Tuna is usually canned in oil, which adds richness to the sauce.
Short‑shaped pasta like penne or rigatoni is traditional, but any shape works.
It is often served with fresh avocado, lime wedges, and cilantro.
Macaroni with tuna is a staple at family gatherings and festive occasions.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Together, tuna and pasta deliver a complete set of essential amino acids for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna is abundant in B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals aid immune function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with tuna in oil or its own brine, the dish remains relatively low in saturated fats.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Tuna can trigger allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Mercury exposure
items.content: Frequent consumption of large amounts of tuna may lead to mercury buildup; moderation is advised.

items.title: Gluten in pasta
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; use gluten‑free alternatives for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the macaroni hot, sprinkled with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, and grated Parmesan. Optional toppings include avocado slices, black olives, or toasted garlic. The dish stores well in the fridge and can be reheated.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though pasta texture may change after thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned peach in a juice pack (item 4013) consists of whole pieces of ripe peach that are hot‑processed and sealed in a hermetic pouch with their own juice. The product retains the natural aroma, sweetness, and nutritional qualities of fresh fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peaches belong to the Rosaceae family and are close relatives of plums, apricots, and cherries.
Canning in the fruit’s own juice preserves up to 80 % of vitamin C compared with other processing methods.
Peaches are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The juice pack made of PET provides a long shelf life without added preservatives.
In many countries canned peaches are traditionally used in desserts such as compote and fruit punches.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and immunity, while vitamin C acts as an antioxidant protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned peaches contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in peaches help combat free radicals.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Many canned peach products contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or low‑carb diets.

items.title: Peach allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peaches, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)
items.content: If the packaging material contains BPA, it could pose a health risk; choose BPA‑free packs when possible.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some manufacturers add preservatives such as potassium sorbate to extend shelf life.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peaches from the pack can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or used in sauces and desserts. Open the pouch and, if desired, drain excess juice before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened pouch in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Unsalted potato chips are thinly sliced potatoes fried or baked until crisp, without any added salt. They retain the natural potato flavor, a slight sweetness, and a crunchy texture. Chips are commonly served as a snack with drinks, in burgers, or as a crunchy topping for salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial production of potato chips began in the United States in the mid‑19th century.
Unsalted chips are often chosen by people watching their sodium intake and by athletes who need to control electrolyte balance.
Potato chips can be prepared by deep‑frying or baking; the latter reduces fat content.
There are many flavored versions—barbecue, cheese, sweet‑spicy—but the unsalted version remains the basic product.
Thin slicing ensures an even golden color when cooked at the right temperature.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply energy, which can be useful before physical activity.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: A small amount of vitamin C survives proper cooking, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which helps regulate fluid balance and muscle function.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: The lack of added salt makes them suitable for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Convenient snack
items.content: They are easy to pack and eat quickly, making them handy for travel and work.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Even without salt, chips are often fried, which makes them calorie‑dense.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Cooking at very high temperatures can produce acrylamides, compounds that may be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to potatoes or to the oils used.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions can cause heaviness due to the high fat content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Unsalted chips can be enjoyed straight from the bag, added to sandwiches, used as a crunchy layer in salads, or served with low‑salt dips. They are convenient for picnics, road trips, and office snacks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to slow fat oxidation. Discard chips that become soft, develop a stale or rancid smell, or change color.
